\chapter{Character, Not Mood}
\label{ch:caracter}
\hlchaptermodality{423}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can describe what a person is like rather than how they feel today, using eight settled-character adjectives and predicting from the spelling alone which of them change ending for a woman.}

Answer the question how is he or she, using es for settled character and letting only the adjectives that can agree do so.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[antipático]{antipático — the opposite made by fastening four letters on the front}

\label{lesson:ES-C423-antipatico}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{simpático}. Now say what you would expect its opposite to look like, before reading on. This is one of the times the obvious guess is right.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item simpático — likeable, and a false friend: it does not mean \emph{sympathetic}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{accent-acute} — \emph{an-ti-PÁ-ti-co}: the written accent sits where the stress does, and adding \emph{anti-} does not move it. $\to$ reference
  \item \texttt{t-dental} — both \textbf{t} sounds are made with the tongue on the teeth, with no puff of air after them.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{antipático} — \textquotedblleft{}unpleasant, disagreeable.\textquotedblright{} Take \emph{simpático} and put Greek \textbf{anti-}, \textquotedblleft{}against, opposite,\textquotedblright{} on the front.

The two Greek prefixes underneath are a pair, and seeing them together makes both words transparent:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{prefix} & \textbf{Greek meaning} & \textbf{with \emph{-pático}} \\
\midrule
sym- & together with & feeling \textbf{with} you \\
anti- & against & feeling \textbf{against} you \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The \emph{-patí-} in the middle is \emph{páthos}, \textquotedblleft{}feeling, suffering\textquotedblright{} — the same piece inside English \textbf{sympathy}, \textbf{empathy} and \textbf{pathetic}.

So \emph{simpático} and \emph{antipático} are literally \emph{feeling-with} and \emph{feeling-against}. Spanish uses them for people who are pleasant and unpleasant to be around, which is a fair everyday translation of the same idea.

\emph{Anti-} is doing exactly the job you already know it does in English: \textbf{anti}biotic, \textbf{anti}septic, \textbf{Anti}arctic — against life, against rot, opposite the Bear.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Both words end in \textbf{-o} and both change ending to match the person:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{masculine} & \textbf{feminine} \\
\midrule
pleasant & simpátic\textbf{o} & simpátic\textbf{a} \\
unpleasant & antipátic\textbf{o} & antipátic\textbf{a} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The prefix never moves and never agrees. Only the last letter does the work.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}antipático\textquotedblright{} — five syllables, stress on \emph{PÁ}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}simpático y antipático\textquotedblright{} one after the other
  \item both in the feminine (\emph{simpática}, \emph{antipática})
  \item which Greek word for feeling is buried in the middle of both (\emph{páthos})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{anti-} mean? (Against.) What does the \emph{-patí-} in the middle mean? (Feeling.) Does the written accent move when the prefix is added? (No — it stays on \emph{PÁ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[inteligente]{inteligente — picking between things, which is all intelligence ever was}

\label{lesson:ES-C423-inteligente}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{alegre}. Notice it ends in \textbf{-e} and never changes for a man or a woman. The word in this lesson does the same thing.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item alegre — cheerful, and the first \textbf{-e} adjective you met that refuses to agree.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{g-soft} — the \textbf{g} in \emph{-gente} comes before \textbf{e}, so it is the throaty sound. \emph{In-te-li-JEN-te}, not \emph{gen} as in English. $\to$ reference
  \item \texttt{stress-penultimate} — stress on \emph{JEN}, the second syllable from the end, and the word carries no written accent because that is already the default.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{inteligente} — \textquotedblleft{}intelligent.\textquotedblright{} Latin \textbf{intellegere}, which is two pieces:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{inter} — between
  \item \textbf{legere} — to gather, to pick out, and later to read
\end{itemize}

To be intelligent is to \textbf{pick between}. Not to know a great deal; to choose well among the things in front of you. The Romans named the ability after the sorting, not after the store of facts.

\emph{Legere} is one of the most productive verbs Latin ever handed over, and every one of these is the same act of picking:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{what is picked} \\
\midrule
\textbf{select} & chosen out (\emph{se-} apart + \emph{legere}) \\
\textbf{collect} & picked together \\
\textbf{elect} & picked out of a group \\
\textbf{legible} & able to be picked out by eye \\
\textbf{lecture} & a reading aloud \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Spanish has them too: \emph{seleccionar}, \emph{colección}, \emph{elegir}, \emph{legible}, \emph{lectura}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two shapes of adjective, side by side:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{ending} & \textbf{masculine} & \textbf{feminine} \\
\midrule
\textbf{-o} & antipátic\textbf{o} & antipátic\textbf{a} \\
\textbf{-e} & inteligente & inteligente \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

An \textbf{-o} adjective has two forms. An \textbf{-e} adjective has one. That is the whole distinction, and it saves you from ever inventing \emph{inteligenta}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}inteligente\textquotedblright{} — \emph{in-te-li-JEN-te}, with the throaty \textbf{g}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}alegre e inteligente\textquotedblright{} — two \textbf{-e} adjectives, neither agreeing
  \item \textquotedblleft{}antipático e inteligente\textquotedblright{} — and hear only the first one able to change
  \item which English word for choosing a leader comes from \emph{legere} (\emph{elect})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two Latin pieces are inside \emph{inteligente}? (\emph{Inter}, between, and \emph{legere}, to pick out.) Does it change for a woman? (No — it ends in \textbf{-e}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[trabajador]{trabajador — the same ending as actor, four hundred years further along}

\label{lesson:ES-C423-trabajador}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{trabajar}. Say \emph{el actor}. One is a verb and one is a person, and this lesson turns the first into the second using the ending the second already showed you.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item trabajar — to work, and a word with a violent past you have already been told about.
  \item el actor — the doer, built with Latin \textbf{-tor}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{stress-final} — \emph{tra-ba-ja-DOR}, stress on the last syllable, exactly as in \emph{actor}. $\to$ reference
  \item \texttt{b-soft} — the \textbf{b} between vowels is soft, with the lips nearly but not quite touching.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{trabajador} — \textquotedblleft{}hard-working.\textquotedblright{} Take \emph{trabajar}, drop the \textbf{-ar}, add \textbf{-dor}.

That ending is the Latin \textbf{-tor} from \emph{actor}, worn down by centuries of Spanish mouths. Latin \emph{-tor} became Spanish \emph{-dor} between vowels, and Spanish then used it on its own verbs to build new words the Romans never had:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{meaning} & \textbf{the one who does it} \\
\midrule
trabajar & to work & trabaja\textbf{dor} \\
jugar & to play & juga\textbf{dor} \\
hablar & to speak & habla\textbf{dor} \\
ganar & to win & gana\textbf{dor} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Actor} was borrowed from Latin whole and kept the old \textbf{-tor}. \emph{Trabajador} was built inside Spanish and got the modern \textbf{-dor}. Same ending, two different ages, and the pair tells you which words came in through books and which grew at home.

Here is the piece that surprises people: \emph{trabajador} is \textbf{both a noun and an adjective}. \emph{Un trabajador} is a worker. \emph{Es trabajador} means he is hard-working. The word does not change; only the sentence around it does.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A third shape of adjective, and it is not the \textbf{-o} one:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{adjective} & \textbf{masculine} & \textbf{feminine} \\
\midrule
antipático & antipático & antipátic\textbf{a} \\
inteligente & inteligente & inteligente \\
trabajador & trabajador & trabajador\textbf{a} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

An adjective ending in a consonant normally refuses to agree. \textbf{-dor} is one of the exceptions that does: it adds \textbf{-a} and nothing else. \emph{Una mujer trabajadora.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}trabajador\textquotedblright{} — \emph{tra-ba-ja-DOR}, stress at the end
  \item \textquotedblleft{}trabajadora\textquotedblright{}, the feminine
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el actor es trabajador\textquotedblright{} — the borrowed ending and the home-grown one in a single sentence
  \item the person-word built from \emph{jugar} the same way (\emph{jugador})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \textbf{-tor} become in home-grown Spanish words? (\textbf{-dor}.) Which of \emph{actor} and \emph{trabajador} came in through books? (\emph{Actor}.) What is the feminine of \emph{trabajador}? (\emph{Trabajadora}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[serio]{serio — the opposite of cheerful, and a word about weight}

\label{lesson:ES-C423-serio}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{alegre}. This lesson gives you the other end of that same scale.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item alegre — cheerful, the word printed on sheet music as \emph{allegro}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{stress-penultimate} — \emph{SE-rio}: \textbf{-io} is a single syllable here, so the stress lands on \emph{SE}. $\to$ reference
  \item \texttt{r-tap} — one flick, between two vowels, which is the easiest place in Spanish to get it right.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{serio} — \textquotedblleft{}serious, earnest.\textquotedblright{} Latin \textbf{serius}, whose first meaning was \textbf{weighty, heavy}.

Every language seems to reach for weight when it wants to talk about gravity of manner, and English does it three separate times without noticing:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a \textbf{grave} matter — Latin \emph{gravis}, heavy
  \item a \textbf{weighty} decision
  \item a matter of some \textbf{gravity}
\end{itemize}

Spanish does the same with \emph{serio} and \emph{grave}. The metaphor is so worn that nobody hears it any more: a serious person is a person who is \textbf{hard to lift}.

One warning worth having. English \emph{serious} has drifted toward meaning \emph{bad} — \emph{a serious accident}. Spanish \emph{serio} stayed with the manner: a \emph{persona seria} is earnest and reliable, not damaged. For the bad kind Spanish uses \emph{grave}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two words for mood and manner, at opposite ends and in different shapes:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{ending} & \textbf{masculine} & \textbf{feminine} \\
\midrule
-e (cheerful) & alegre & alegre \\
-o (serious) & seri\textbf{o} & seri\textbf{a} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

You now have both ends of the scale, and each one demonstrates a different agreement rule.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}serio\textquotedblright{} — \emph{SE-rio}, two syllables
  \item \textquotedblleft{}seria\textquotedblright{}, the feminine
  \item \textquotedblleft{}alegre y serio\textquotedblright{} — the pair, one agreeing and one not
  \item \textquotedblleft{}trabajador y serio\textquotedblright{} — two consonant-ending and \textbf{-o}-ending adjectives together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{serius} first mean? (Weighty, heavy.) Does Spanish \emph{serio} mean \emph{grave} in the sense of a bad accident? (No — that is \emph{grave}.) How many syllables is \emph{serio}? (Two: \emph{SE-rio}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tímido]{tímido — fear, and the verb for putting it into somebody}

\label{lesson:ES-C423-timido}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{serio}. A serious person and a shy person look similar from the outside and are nothing alike inside. This lesson names the second one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item serio — earnest, from Latin for \emph{weighty}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{accent-acute} — \emph{TÍ-mi-do}: the accent marks the stress on the third syllable from the end, which Spanish always writes out. $\to$ reference
  \item \texttt{t-dental} — tongue against the teeth, no puff of air. An English \emph{t} here is the single clearest giveaway of an English speaker.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{tímido} — \textquotedblleft{}shy, timid.\textquotedblright{} Latin \textbf{timidus}, from the verb \textbf{timere}, \textquotedblleft{}to fear.\textquotedblright{}

\emph{Timere} built a small family, and English took all of it:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{literally} \\
\midrule
\textbf{timid} & inclined to fear \\
\textbf{timorous} & full of fear \\
\textbf{intimidate} & to put fear \textbf{into} someone \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That last one is the useful one. \emph{In-} means \emph{into}. To \textbf{intimidate} somebody is to place the fear inside them — the exact fear that \emph{tímido} names. The shy person and the bully are described with the same Latin root, from opposite ends.

Spanish keeps the whole family too: \emph{tímido}, \emph{temer} (to fear), \emph{intimidar}.

A note on what the word does \textbf{not} say. \emph{Tímido} describes how a person meets strangers, not whether they are frightened at this moment. For being afraid right now, Spanish says \emph{tener miedo}. This is settled character, which is the whole point of the chapter.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three \textbf{-o} adjectives now, all agreeing the same way:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{masculine} & \textbf{feminine} \\
\midrule
antipático & antipática \\
serio & seria \\
tímido & tímida \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two of the three carry a written accent, and in both cases the accent stays exactly where it was when the ending changes: \emph{tímido} $\to$ \emph{tímida}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tímido\textquotedblright{} — \emph{TÍ-mi-do}, stress on the first of three
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tímida\textquotedblright{}, and notice the accent has not moved
  \item \textquotedblleft{}serio y tímido\textquotedblright{}
  \item which English verb means to put fear into someone (\emph{intimidate})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does Latin \emph{timere} mean? (To fear.) What does the \emph{in-} of \emph{intimidate} add? (Into — putting the fear into someone.) Does \emph{tímido} mean frightened right now? (No — that is \emph{tener miedo}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sociable]{sociable — a companion, an ending, and the strangest word in English sport}

\label{lesson:ES-C423-sociable}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{tímido}. Now say the opposite kind of person, and expect the word to look almost exactly like its English twin.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item tímido — shy, from Latin for fear.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{stress-penultimate} — \emph{so-CIA-ble}, stress on the second syllable from the end and no written accent, because that is the default. $\to$ reference
  \item \texttt{b-soft} — the \textbf{b} is soft, between a vowel and an \textbf{l}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{sociable} — \textquotedblleft{}sociable, outgoing.\textquotedblright{} Latin \textbf{socius}, \textquotedblleft{}a companion, an ally, a sharer,\textquotedblright{} plus \textbf{-able}, \textquotedblleft{}able to be, inclined to.\textquotedblright{}

\emph{Socius} is one of those roots that turns out to be everywhere:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{the companion in it} \\
\midrule
\textbf{society} & the whole body of companions \\
\textbf{associate} & to make someone a companion \\
\textbf{social} & to do with companions \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

And then there is the one nobody expects. English \emph{association football} was shortened by Oxford students, who liked adding \textbf{-er} to clipped words, into \textbf{soccer} — from \emph{assoc}. The most ordinary word in world sport has \emph{socius} sitting inside it, meaning nothing more than \emph{companion}.

Spanish has the family too: \emph{la sociedad}, \emph{social}, \emph{el socio} — which is a business partner or a club member, and is \emph{socius} almost unchanged after two thousand years.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The six character words of this chapter sort into three agreement shapes, and now you have seen all three:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{shape} & \textbf{example} & \textbf{feminine} \\
\midrule
\textbf{-o} & tímido & tímida \\
\textbf{-e} & inteligente & inteligente \\
\textbf{-able} & sociable & sociable \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{-able} behaves like \textbf{-e}: one form for everyone. A \emph{hombre sociable} and a \emph{mujer sociable}, spelled identically.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sociable\textquotedblright{} — \emph{so-CIA-ble}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tímido y sociable\textquotedblright{} — the two ends of the same trait
  \item \textquotedblleft{}inteligente y sociable\textquotedblright{} — both invariable
  \item which English sport hides \emph{socius} in its name (\emph{soccer})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{socius} mean? (A companion or ally.) Does \emph{sociable} change for a woman? (No — \textbf{-able} has one form.) Which everyday Spanish word for a club member is \emph{socius} barely changed? (\emph{El socio}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ocho palabras de carácter]{ocho palabras de carácter — eight words, three endings, two pairs}

\label{lesson:ES-C423-repaso-caracter}



\begin{quote}
Name as many of the eight as you can before reading the table. Aim for six.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the ending decides whether the word can move}]
All eight, sorted by what their last letters allow:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{meaning} & \textbf{feminine} \\
\midrule
simpático & likeable & simpática \\
antipático & unpleasant & antipática \\
serio & earnest & seria \\
tímido & shy & tímida \\
trabajador & hard-working & trabajadora \\
alegre & cheerful & alegre \\
inteligente & clever & inteligente \\
sociable & outgoing & sociable \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read the third column against the first. Where the two differ, the word moves for a woman; where they are identical, it does not.

Five move and three do not, and you can predict which from the spelling alone: a word ending in \textbf{-o} changes, a word ending in \textbf{-e} does not, and \textbf{-dor} is the consonant ending that changes anyway.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two of them are matched opposites}]
Four of the eight come in pairs, which halves what there is to remember:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{one end} & \textbf{other end} & \textbf{what the pair measures} \\
\midrule
simpático & antipático & how you are to be around \\
tímido & sociable & how you meet strangers \\
alegre & serio & how you carry yourself \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three scales, six words. \emph{Inteligente} and \emph{trabajador} stand alone.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the five that change, in their feminine forms
  \item the three that do not change
  \item each pair as an opposite — \emph{simpático, antipático}; \emph{tímido, sociable}; \emph{alegre, serio}
  \item the two that have no partner (\emph{inteligente}, \emph{trabajador})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which consonant ending agrees anyway? (\textbf{-dor}, as in \emph{trabajadora}.) Which two of the eight are not one half of a pair? (\emph{Inteligente} and \emph{trabajador}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[¿Cómo es?]{¿Cómo es? — the question these eight words exist to answer}

\label{lesson:ES-C423-sintesis-persona}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{inteligente} and \emph{trabajador}. Two words a reference letter cannot do without, and you have had neither until now.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: es for character, está for the moment}]
Spanish has two verbs where English has one, and character is the clean half of the split:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{what it reports} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
\textbf{es} & settled character & \emph{Es tímido.} — He is a shy person. \\
\textbf{está} & how someone is right now & \emph{Está alegre.} — He is cheerful today. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

All eight of these adjectives are about settled character, so all eight take \textbf{es}. That is what makes them exam adjectives rather than mood adjectives: a question asking \emph{¿Cómo es tu hermano?} wants the lasting answer.

\emph{Alegre} is the one that can honestly go either way — \emph{es alegre} is a cheerful person, \emph{está alegre} is a person having a good day.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
Read aloud. Every word has been taught:

\begin{quote}
— ¿Cómo es tu hermana? — Es simpática e inteligente. Es un poco tímida, pero es muy trabajadora. — ¿Y tu hermano? — No es antipático, pero es muy serio.
\end{quote}

Two things to catch. \emph{Y} becomes \textbf{e} before a word starting with the \emph{i} sound — \emph{simpática \textbf{e} inteligente} — because \emph{y inteligente} would blur into one vowel. And every adjective describing \emph{hermana} has taken its \textbf{-a}, while the ones that cannot change have stayed put.
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}¿Cómo es?\textquotedblright{} and answer it with three of the eight
  \item the same three describing a woman, changing only the ones that can change
  \item \textquotedblleft{}es simpática e inteligente\textquotedblright{} and hear why it is not \emph{y}
  \item one sentence about somebody you know, using \emph{es} and two adjectives
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the two verbs does settled character take? (\emph{Es}.) Why does \emph{y} become \emph{e} before \emph{inteligente}? (The following word begins with the \emph{i} sound, and the two vowels would run together.) Which of the eight can honestly take either verb? (\emph{Alegre}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
